summary: Technical deep dive focused on a recent series of OOMs and timeouts Atlas observed when running long conversations in their VPC private deployment. Covered retry semantics, CUDA OOM patterns, KV cache behavior during high concurrency, batching tradeoffs, and quantization impact. Agreed next steps: run targeted repro, share logs, and tune batching/KV cache; Redwood to propose Dedicated pilot sizing.
topics: OOM root causes (CUDA memory fragmentation / peak allocations)
KV cache eviction behavior under burst traffic
VPC/on-prem nuances (driver versions, MIG, node sizing)
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, we'll focus on the OOMs you've been seeing in the private VPC setup and walk through retry semantics and possible mitigations. Tom will take the technical lead.
[00:20] Rajesh: Thanks, yeah we've had intermittent CUDA OOMs when we push long convos, usually at peak qps, sometimes we also see timeouts which then trigger retries and more load so it cascades.
[00:35] Tom: ok, can you describe the pattern — is it all at startup, or during steady state?
[00:42] Maya: Mostly steady state. it's more reproducible with seq lengths around 512 to 1k tokens, and bursty traffic ~80-120 concurrent requests. Usually on our rtx A100 nodes in the VPC.
[00:57] Tom: thanks. first thought is memory fragmentation + kv cache growth. when KV entries accumulate for many unique prefixes you can hit peak device memory even if average token length is lower. are you pinning model weights to GPU and using per-request KV cache on the same device?
[01:18] Rajesh: yes weights+kv on the same GPU, no offload. we tried setting smaller max_batch_size but that didn't fully resolve it.
[01:26] Lena: two quick items — one is allocator fragmentation: long-running processes on CUDA can fragment memory; the other is transient spikes from batching behavior. if a retry causes a request to re-enter the queue, it can produce a short burst that inflates the batch beyond expected.
[01:44] Oliver: we also saw a pattern where a single request with 2048 tokens triggers a large KV cache, then eviction churn happens and sometimes the server takes a long GC-like pause, which looks like a timeout.
[01:56] Tom: that matches. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching and automatic KV caching by session. If eviction policy isn't tuned to your prefix churn, you'll get high memory usage. quick question — are you using session affinity for chat sessions or purely stateless requests?
[02:10] Maya: session affinity via sticky cookies, but the conversation ids vary a lot.
[02:16] Tom: ok. recommended short-term: set a soft cap on per-session KV entries, enable prefix-level pruning after N tokens, and set a conservative max_concurrent_batches to avoid burst amplification. We'll share concrete config.
[02:32] Rajesh: about timeouts — our client side retries after 3s. if the server is overloaded, retries just double the load. is there a built-in retry backoff in Redwood endpoints?
[02:45] Aisha: good point. the hosted API has exponential backoff semantics we recommend; in private deployments you control the client retry policy. Tom, do we have a recommended pattern?
[02:54] Tom: yes, avoid immediate client retries on 5xx or timeout — use jittered exponential backoff and ideally idempotency keys for duplicate suppression. also consider server-side rate limiting to shed load and return 429 rather than letting retries cascade.
[03:10] Sophie: from a security/compliance side we also need to keep audit logs for retries and error codes, can Redwood expose those in the Private control plane?
[03:18] Lena: yes the private control plane includes request tracing and error histograms; we can surface GPU-level OOM stack traces if permitted by your security policy — some customers restrict stack trace export.
[03:31] Rajesh: curious about CUDA driver versions — we've been on 11.4 but engineering suggests 11.8 or 12.x is more stable. does Redwood require a specific driver for Private?
[03:40] Tom: we recommend matching driver and cuDNN versions validated for the runtime. for the recent kernels we shipped, 11.7+ or 12.1 are preferred; older drivers show more fragmentation and kernel fallback. we'll share a supported matrix.
[03:53] Maya: good. another question: quantization — we moved to int8 for cost, but we see occasional target hallucinations and some instability in token timing. could quantization be contributing to OOM patterns?
[04:07] Tom: quantization primarily affects memory footprint for weights and can reduce peak memory; it shouldn't directly cause OOMs unless the quantized kernels allocate different workspace sizes on CUDA. but it can change performance characteristics; some kernels use extra workspace and trigger transient spikes. Also int8 kernel availability depends on CUDA and the compute capability (MIG/shared memory behavior on A100s).
[04:30] Oliver: we run mixed workloads, some short embeddings + long chat. might batching for embeddings interact badly with chat requests?
[04:38] Lena: yes mixed request types can lead to suboptimal batching and memory spikes. recommend separate queues or classify routes — e.g., embeddings to dedicated pool or dedicate a subset of GPUs with smaller batch windows.
[04:53] Rajesh: about retries — we saw repeated "CUDA out of memory" logs followed by a number of automatic retries from our client. Is there a Redwood server-side retry for failed inferences?
[05:03] Tom: server-side we have retry semantics for transient infra errors but we avoid automatic re-running of in-flight generation since that's non-idempotent. what you're likely seeing is client retries. we can surface specific 5xx vs 4xx codes so clients can back off.
[05:18] Maya: any guidance around max tokens and concurrency on A100 80GB vs A100 40GB?
[05:25] Tom: rough ballpark: for 80GB you can run many more concurrent 512-token streams; for 40GB plan for fewer concurrent long sequences or consider model sharding + kv offload. We'll include a sizing table.
[05:36] Sophie: is there support for GPU memory overcommit or spill-to-host?
[05:41] Lena: we do have an optional CPU spill path for KV cache in Private deployments, but spill increases latency and may affect tail SLOs — useful as a safety net. also there's an on-disk spilling prototype but not recommended for low-latency production.
[05:56] Rajesh: could you explain a concrete repro plan so we can reproduce in our env?
[06:01] Tom: yes — run a 2h workload with these parameters: seq lengths 512/1024 mix (70/30), concurrency ramp to 120 qps sustained, with bursts to 180 for 30s; enable full KV cache, and capture nvidia-smi -i, dmesg, and runtime logs at debug. We'll provide a script.
[06:22] Aisha: we'll attach the repro script and Tom will run it in Redwood's test harness too to compare traces.
[06:29] Rajesh: one more item — we saw a pattern where the allocator logs show many small allocations before the OOM, looks like fragmentation. any allocator tuning?
[06:38] Lena: we can recommend setting the CUDA memory pool and enabling caching allocator trimming on interval to reduce fragmentation; also restart cadence can help but isn't ideal. Another lever is to avoid many small allocations by using larger pre-allocated buffers for KV entries.
[06:56] Maya: about the KV eviction policy — what's default? LRU?
[07:00] Tom: default is time-based + soft-lru. for high-churn prefix workloads we recommend a fixed-size per-session ring buffer with TTL on entries to bound memory.
[07:12] Oliver: Could we get a config example?
[07:15] Tom: yes, we'll share config snippets — e.g., per_session_kv_limit=500 entries, eviction_ttl=1800s, max_concurrent_batches=8. Those are starting points.
[07:33] Sophie: on VPC networking — we've seen timeouts due to node-level MTU misconfiguration and occasional packet fragmentation; that can look like timeouts on the app layer. Any network checks?
[07:45] Lena: check kernel NIC offload settings (GRO/LRO), MTU, and ensure keepalives are tuned. For Private we also recommend using ENA drivers on AWS and correct CNI settings to avoid high tail latency.
[08:00] Rajesh: what about model fallbacks — can Redwood route to a smaller model automatically when capacity is constrained?
[08:07] Aisha: yes that's one of our smart routing patterns. you can configure fallback to a quantized or smaller variant when latency/backpressure is detected.
[08:16] Maya: would that change output semantics badly? we need to preserve quality.
[08:20] Tom: that's why rollouts and A/B testing are recommended — define success metrics and automatic rollback if quality drops. Also quality guards can prevent fallback for certain sessions.
[08:33] Rajesh: logging — we need clear error labels to correlate client retries to OOMs. Can Redwood add GPU OOM metrics to trace ids in logs?
[08:42] Lena: yes we correlate OOM events with request ids and surface them in the control plane; we can mask stack traces if needed for compliance.
[08:52] Aisha: ok let's go into a few specific logs you shared earlier (Aisha screen shares).
[09:00] [screen share noise]
[09:10] Tom: I see repeated pattern: alloc 7.9GiB, free 7.9GiB, then large spike 23.4GiB before OOM — that's consistent with a single large KV insertion. Are any of your clients sending extremely long single messages?
[09:26] Maya: sometimes users paste docs into the chat, so yes. We do have limits but not yet enforced upstream.
[09:32] Tom: enforce server-side max_input_tokens and early reject long requests — that prevents single requests from blowing memory. Also apply per-request workspace limits.
[09:42] Rajesh: on retries again, we changed client from 3 retries to 1 and saw fewer cascades but OOMs still happen.
[09:49] Tom: reduce client retries and add adaptive backoff based on 429/503 ratio; server should emit 429 when overloaded.
[09:58] Oliver: what's Redwood's guidance on kernel versions for quantized int8 on A100?
[10:04] Tom: ensure CUDA 11.7+ and cuBLAS/cuDNN versions that match our kernel build; we supply a compatibility matrix. int8 kernels sometimes require newer drivers.
[10:15] Maya: are there any known issues with MIG on A100 and memory accounting?
[10:21] Lena: MIG isolates memory, but some kernels assume monolithic GPU and can fail or be suboptimal on MIG slices; be cautious, and test on your specific MIG profile.
[10:33] Rajesh: ok, let's recap actions.
[10:35] Aisha: recap: 1) Tom to share repro script + run on Redwood harness; 2) Atlas to run repro in VPC and share nvlog/dmesg; 3) Lena to share KV/batching tuning doc; 4) Aisha to send pilot SOW and pricing.
[10:50] Tom: one more tactical note — consider lowering max_batch_size and increasing batch frequency (smaller batches more often) to reduce peak allocation spikes; it's a tradeoff with throughput.
[11:02] Maya: noted. any final security notes?
[11:06] Sophie: ensure any shared logs strip PII, and we need RBAC on exported traces.
[11:12] Lena: acknowledged, we'll sanitize before sharing.
[11:18] Aisha: great, we'll follow up with the links. thanks all.
[11:22] [meeting ends]
